question: The majority of anterior epistaxis in adults arises from Little's area (Kiesselbach's plexus) on the anterior nasal septum, which is why anterior nasal packing and direct pressure are effective first-line treatments for most nosebleeds.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is true. Little's area (Kiesselbach's plexus) = anteroinferior septum = site of approximately 90% of all nosebleeds. That is why simple first-aid measures (pinching the nose, anterior packing) are usually effective. Posterior epistaxis from the sphenopalatine artery is less common but more severe and less responsive to simple anterior compression.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. Little's area (Kiesselbach's plexus) on the anteroinferior nasal septum is a vascular watershed zone supplied by four arteries: the anterior ethmoidal artery (from ophthalmic artery), the sphenopalatine artery, the greater palatine artery, and the superior labial artery. Its superficial, easily traumatised position makes it responsible for approximately 90% of anterior epistaxis. Direct pressure (pinching the soft cartilaginous part of the nose for 10-15 minutes) and anterior nasal packing work precisely because they compress this region.
